greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
hint: Closed, the first three letters are the same three that open Genesis. That is the point of the verse.

notes.text: Word for word the opening of LXX Genesis. John is quoting the *Greek* Old Testament, not the Hebrew. On a Septuagint base the citation is simply visible on the page instead of buried in a footnote — which is the whole argument for reading the Old Testament in Greek alongside the New.

Imperfect of εἰμί — and emphatically *not* ἐγένετο, *came to be*, which the prologue reserves for created things from verse 3 onward. The entire architecture of the passage rests on this one contrast, and English *was* carries none of it. Hence the expansion: *was already in unbroken existence without any point of having come to be*.

Articular. The range: the spoken word, the utterance, the thing said; the account or reckoning, as in rendering an account; ratio and proportion; reasoned discourse; and in Stoic usage the rational principle ordering the cosmos. English *Word* keeps the speech and drops the reason. Latin had the same problem — *verbum* won, though *sermo* held more.

πρός with the accusative is directional: toward, facing, up against. It is not παρά (beside), not μετά (in company with), not σύν (together with) — any of which the writer could have used. English *with* is static; πρός is vectored. This is the largest single loss in the standard versions.

The predicate θεός stands without the article and is thrown to the front; ὁ λόγος carries the article and is the subject. A fronted anarthrous predicate nominative is normally *qualitative* — it says what the subject is by nature, not which individual it is identical with. So: not *the Word was the Father*, which the article placement refuses, and not *a god*, which the fronting refuses. Word order does work here that no English word order can do, which is why this clause has been fought over for eighteen centuries.
λόγος and its chain are printed lowercase. The manuscripts have no lower case, so the capital in the familiar *Word* is not in the text; it is an editorial decision that the noun is a title.
None. λόγος is expanded, not transliterated.

greek: οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν.
hint: Six words, and every one of them has already appeared in verse 1.

notes.text: Near demonstrative — *this one here*. It gathers up everything just said and pins it to one referent, which is why the expansion adds *and no other*.

It restates 1a and 1b together, and its work is to block a reading in which the θεός of 1c is a different party from the τὸν θεόν of 1b. The one who is God by nature is the same one who stands face to face toward God. The verse looks redundant in English and is not redundant in Greek.
The fourth imperfect in two verses. Still no ἐγένετο. The writer is being relentless, and a version that renders all four as a flat *was* hides the relentlessness.
None in this verse.

greek: πάντα διʼ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν. ὃ γέγονεν
hint: Everything, the verse says, came to be through him. Where its last two words belong is a question of punctuation.

notes.text: Aorist of γίνομαι, *came to be*: the verb verses 1–2 kept from the Logos is now given to everything else. The verse says it twice, once positively and once with χωρίς, *apart from*.
διά with the genitive, *through*: the Logos is the agency, not the source. The writer could have used ὑπό (*by*) or ἐκ (*out of*) and did not.

SBLGNT puts the full stop before ὃ γέγονεν, so the words open verse 4: *what has come to be, in him was life*. Placed after them, they close verse 3: *apart from him came to be not one thing that has come to be*. The earliest manuscripts carry no punctuation; both readings construe. γέγονεν is perfect: a state that stands, beside the aorist ἐγένετο.

greek: ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων·
hint: Life was in him, and that life was the light of men: two more ἦν, none of them ἐγένετο.

notes.text: Twice imperfect of εἰμί, and so the prologue's formula twice. Created things γίνονται; the life in the Logos is said to be, not to have come to be.
Middle Liddell files φῶς as the contracted φάος: *light, daylight*, *a light*. The plural's *eyes* belongs to the plural and is left out.
Anarthrous first, then articular: *life* is introduced, then *the life* is that life, named again.

greek: καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν.
hint: The light shines on in the dark, present tense; the dark did not lay hold of it, aorist.

notes.text: Present active: the light's shining goes on. Middle Liddell gives the active its intransitive *to give light, shine* beside the causative *to bring to light*, which heads.

Aorist of καταλαμβάνω. The range holds both *to seize, overtake* and *to seize with the mind, apprehend, comprehend*: the dark did not overcome it, or did not grasp it. The Greek does not choose and the chain keeps both.
Neuter, agreeing with φῶς: *it*, the light.

greek: Ἐγένετο ἄνθρωπος ἀπεσταλμένος παρὰ θεοῦ, ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης·
hint: The sentence opens with the verb the Logos was never given.

notes.text: Aorist middle of γίνομαι — *came to be, came into existence, arose*. Placed first for emphasis. This is precisely the verb withheld from the Logos in verses 1–2, and it arrives the moment a creature enters the sentence.
Perfect passive participle of ἀποστέλλω — sent off on another's authority, dispatched with a commission. The perfect makes it a standing status, not a past errand. Root of ἀπόστολος.

A Greek transliteration of Hebrew *Yôḥānān*, a compound of the divine name with the verb *ḥānan*, to show favour or be gracious: *Yah has shown favour*. The name is kept in the Greek form and glossed in parentheses. It is not translated away, because it is what the man was called; it is not left bare, because to the first hearers it was a sentence.

demo.note: None of the four verses above contains a proper name, so here is the naming rule working on the first one the prologue offers — a verse that also puts the ἦν / ἐγένετο contrast on display.

hint: The man of verse 6 came for witness: two purpose clauses, one for the witness, one for those who would trust.

notes.text: εἰς with the accusative: *for* or *into* witness, the purpose of the coming. μαρτυρία and μαρτυρέω, the witness and the bearing of it, recur through the chapter.

greek: ἦν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ὃ φωτίζει πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐρχόμενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον.
hint: Whether 'coming into the world' belongs to the light or to every man, the participle's form allows both.

notes.text: The form is neuter nominative or masculine accusative. Neuter, it goes with τὸ φῶς and with ἦν: *the true light … was coming into the world*. Masculine, it goes with ἄνθρωπον: *every man coming into the world*. MorphGNT parses it masculine; the grammar does not decide.
The adjective carries its own article, so its unit takes *the*: *the light, the true one*. ἀληθινός, *agreeable to truth*, is genuine as against counterfeit, not ἀληθής, *true* as against false.
κόσμος heads with *order*: an arrangement, then an ornament, then the ordered whole, the world. The chain keeps the range.

greek: Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν, καὶ ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός, πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας·
hint: The Logos now takes ἐγένετο, the verb withheld from it: it came to be flesh and pitched its tent 'among us'.

notes.text: The verb verses 1–2 withheld from the Logos, now given it: not ἦν but ἐγένετο. σάρξ is anarthrous, the predicate.
Aorist of σκηνόω, *to pitch a tent*, from σκηνή: the word for Exodus's tent of witness, ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου, which stands in the corpus (EXO 26–40).
δόξα heads with *notion, expectation, opinion*, its classical sense; *glory* is the Septuagint's use of it for Hebrew kābôd, which Middle Liddell gives further down the entry.
Nominative, though the nearest nouns are accusative and genitive. It may go with ὁ λόγος, or πλήρης was by this period used indeclinably. The grammar does not decide.

notes.text: Neuter plural of οὗτος, *these*: the exchange of 19–27.

greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ⸀ὑμῖν, ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
hint: Amen, amen: heaven opened and God's messengers going up and down, Jacob's ladder from Genesis 28:12.

notes.text: Genesis 28:12 in the Septuagint: οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνέβαινον καὶ κατέβαινον ἐπʼ αὐτῆς, on the ladder. Here they go up and down ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. GEN 28:12 stands in the corpus, the same verbs in the same order.
From Hebrew ʾāmēn, *firm, sure*, said to affirm: a transliteration, glossed as a name. Doubled, it opens a solemn saying, here for the first time in the book.
ἄγγελος heads with *a messenger*: one sent with word, before the heavenly sense.
Perfect participle of ἀνοίγω: heaven opened and standing open.
